title: Radio listening in Columbus
summary: Radio meant scary stories and late-night bands from far away; Monk was not an attentive listener, though he recalls Andy Kirk and Chick Webb.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: And then he began by himself, from there?
Right there. I'm telling you. I wasn't, like I said, into music or tuned in at that age. I wasn't tuned in...
Not at all? Did you listen to the radio?

But Wes...Oh, yeah, we listened to radio. You know, there was all there was to listen to. We listened to...We had a radio. My dad had one of those floor model radios, the big floor model that...I guess it needed some repair work on it because it would go in and out, the sound would go in and out.
What did you listen to on it?
Well, we'd listen to those bands, the late night things coming from faraway places like Chicago. And there were

...it wasn't that he was a radio listener. He listened and didn't listen; he heard and didn't hear. There was no...you go to the radio to turn to a certain station because there's a certain program. The program had to do with scary stories. There was a lot of that; there was more of that in radio...
So you didn't especially use it to tune in to the bands?

No, there wasn't a whole lot of bands to be tuned. The traffic of music wasn't like it is. There were some to be heard, but Columbus wasn't popular [with the bands], of course. Like I say, I remember that there were stations in Louisville, or in faraway places. But there were times when, on Saturdays I think it was, mainly, you could hear a lot of jazz and bands. And the bands were like...I remember Andy Kirk and I remember } Chick Webb, and I remember, naturally, all the people in that era.
